[Thinking]
**Clarifying user needs**

The user’s question is a bit broad, so I need to ask for more specific details. I should inquire about the engine type, symptoms, make/model, and whether it’s fresh or saltwater. Knowing if it’s outboard or inboard, two-stroke or four-stroke, as well as their tools and experience is crucial.

I’ll also want to provide general troubleshooting steps, safety precautions, common problems, fixes, and advice on when to consult a professional. Keeping everything concise will be essential! A checklist for diagnostics and basic fixes sounds like a great idea.
[/Thinking]

I can help — but “fix my boat engine” is very broad. To give useful, safe guidance I need details. Answer the short checklist below, then I’ll give targeted steps based on what’s wrong:

Please tell me:
- Engine type: outboard or inboard (stern drive?) — and brand/model/year if known.
- Fuel type: gasoline or diesel.
- 2‑stroke or 4‑stroke (if known).
- Symptoms: what exactly is happening? (won’t start, hard starting, stalls, runs rough, overheating, poor power, oil leak, smoking, vibration, gear/prop issues, etc.)
- When did the problem start and any events (ran out of fuel, winter layup, trailer launch, saltwater exposure)?
- Any recent work, noises, smells, warning lights, or gauges abnormal?
- Your skill level and tools available (basic tools, multimeter, compression tester, lift/hoist, shore power).

General safety first
- Work on a trailer or stable dock; be sure engine is out of gear, ignition off, battery disconnected when working on electrical/fuel system.
- Use adequate ventilation when running engine; avoid enclosed spaces.
- Wear eye/hand protection and follow fuel/fire safety.
- If the boat’s on the water and you’re stranded, call for towing/rescue rather than trying major repairs.

Quick basic troubleshooting checklist (do these first)
1. Battery/electrical:
   - Check battery voltage (12.6V+ fully charged). At crank should not drop below ~10V.
   - Clean battery terminals and connections. Tighten ground straps.
   - Try a jump-start or known-good battery.

2. Fuel:
   - Ensure you have fresh, correct fuel and the tank valve is open.
   - Check fuel level and fuel line for kinks/air leaks.
   - Replace inline fuel filter and inspect primer bulb for soft/damaged/air leaks.
   - If suspected stale fuel, drain or siphon and add fresh fuel; run fuel system with recommended stabilizer/biocide if bacterial growth suspected.

3. Ignition/spark:
   - For gasoline outboards, pull a spark plug to check condition and spark. Replace fouled plugs.
   - Check spark plug wires/coil packs and ignition switch/kill switch/lanyard.
   - If no spark, test ignition coil and kill circuit.

4. Air intake/filters:
   - Check air cleaner for blockages (inboards) and make sure cowling vents are clear (outboards).
   - Throttle linkage free and choke operation correct.

5. Cooling/overheating:
   - Check raw-water pump impeller (replace if worn/cracked).
   - Ensure water intake strainer and raw-water intake aren’t blocked; look for telltale stream of cooling water from tell-tale (if equipped).
   - Check thermostat (inboard/sterndrive) and coolant level (closed-cooling systems).

6. Fuel delivery (carburetor vs EFI):
   - Carburetor: old fuel varnish can clog jets — consider carb cleaning or rebuild.
   - EFI: check fuel pressure to spec and electrical connectors.

7. Compression/mechanical:
   - Low compression causes hard starting and poor power. Use compression tester to compare cylinders. If low, inspect head gasket, valves, pistons.
   - Unusual noises (knock, rattle) — stop running engine and get professional diagnosis.

8. Lower unit / prop:
   - Check prop for damage and fishing-line wrapped around prop shaft causing overheating and seal damage.
   - Inspect lower unit oil for water contamination (milky color) indicating seal failure.

Common specific fixes
- Engine won’t crank: check battery, starter solenoid, ignition switch, neutral safety switch, and ground connections.
- Cranks but won’t start: fuel delivery (fuel pump, clogged filter), no spark, flooded engine (dry spark plugs and try again), choke operation.
- Starts then dies or idles rough: carburetor/EFI issues, dirty fuel, vacuum leaks, fouled plugs, bad idle adjustment.
- Overheating: impeller replacement, thermostat, clogged raw-water passages, blocked exhaust.
- Smoke:
   - Blue: burning oil (rings, valve guides, excessive oil in two-stroke mix).
   - White: coolant in combustion (head gasket) or water ingestion.
   - Black: rich fuel mixture or clogged air filter.

Tools & parts commonly needed
- Basic mechanic’s toolset, socket set, screwdrivers, pliers.
- Multimeter, fuel pressure gauge, compression tester.
- Spare spark plugs, fuel filter(s), inline primer bulb, impeller, lower unit oil, gear lube pump, owner’s manual/service manual.

When to call a mechanic
- If compression is low.
- Head gasket or internal engine damage suspected.
- Major oil contamination, broken crank/connecting rod noise.
- You’re unsure and on the water — towing is safer.
- Complex EFI diagnostics requiring dealer tools or ECM programming.

If you tell me your engine type, brand/model, and the exact symptoms/situation now, I’ll give a step-by-step troubleshooting and repair plan specific to your case.
